title: The Pretesting Effect Is Robust Throughout Adulthood, But Metacognitive Beliefs About Pretesting and Challenge Differ https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1041608025000597
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), May 28, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Yan, Duany Rea and Sana's two-study investigation into whether the pretesting effect, the memory boost from guessing before being taught, holds up across the entire adult lifespan (18 to 82/83 years), and how beliefs about it differ by age. The cognitive benefit itself turns out to be remarkably stable, unmoderated by age or memory contentment, across roughly 570 participants recruited via Prolific. What does change with age is metacognitive belief: younger adults are more likely to appreciate the value of guessing and making errors, while middle-aged and older adults are less likely to see errors and challenge as beneficial, creating a metacognitive mismatch where the group that could benefit most is least likely to choose the strategy. Barton draws out that lifelong learning support needs to do two separate jobs, teach the technique, and separately reshape learners' attitudes toward productive struggle, with the second job mattering more as learners age.
points: The pretesting effect is stable across the entire adult lifespan (18 to over 80), not moderated by age or self-reported memory contentment.
Younger adults appreciate the value of guessing and errorful learning more than middle-aged and older adults, despite the cognitive benefit being equal across ages.
This creates a metacognitive mismatch: older adults benefit just as much from pretesting but are less likely to choose it, because they undervalue the strategy.
About a quarter of participants actually scored lower on pretested items than study-only items, showing the technique isn't universally beneficial for every individual.
Supporting lifelong learning requires not just teaching effective techniques like pretesting, but actively reshaping learners' attitudes toward errors and challenge, especially for older learners.
quotes: The research, conducted across a wide age range, found that the pretesting effect—the learning benefit from making initial guesses, even incorrect ones—remained consistent throughout adulthood.

The study highlights a significant difference in metacognitive beliefs about this strategy, revealing that while younger adults tend to see the value in pretesting and making errors, older adults are less likely to appreciate the benefits of this errorful learning.
Younger participants were more likely to appreciate the benefits of pretesting than middle-aged and older adults.
The findings reveal a metacognitive mismatch where older adults underestimate the effectiveness of a strategy (pretesting/errorful learning) that is actually beneficial for them.
Approximately 25% of participants in Study 1 actually scored lower on the pretested items compared to study-only items.

These findings highlight the importance of shifting attitudes towards challenge to support desirably difficult approaches to learning, thus ensuring that learners have both the right mindset and the right toolset
